newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Swiss franc falls further in active Asian trading.
newsitem.headline: Swiss franc falls further in active Asian trading.

text.p: The Swiss franc continued to weaken in active trading during the Asian morning on Tuesday following overnight remarks by Switzerland's finance minister which led to a flood of selling, dealers said.
"It's open season on the Swissie at the moment. Right now it just seems to be a one way bet. I have no idea when we'll reach a bottom," said the head trader at a European firm in Singapore.
At 0322 GMT, the Swiss franc was quoted at 1.4360/70 against the dollar compared with a close in Zurich on Monday of 1.4144/50 and a New York finish of 1.4300/05.
The Swiss franc's retreat began after Swiss Finance Minister Kaspar Villiger told a wire service in an interview that he was "relieved" with the recent weakness in the currency.
The trader said this remark had a dramatic effect, although it was entirely consistent with recent efforts by the Swiss National Bank to push the currency lower.
"The selling started in Switzerland, New York were happy to carry it on and Asia are maintaining the trend," he said.
A trader at another European bank said he was having his busiest day in a long time. "When a finance minister tells you to sell his currency, you do it," he said.

He added he had seen no real signs of support although he said there could be technical support at the 1.4360 level. "It's tried to get through once and not made it, but this is one of those day's when technicals don't count for much," he said.
Steve Shuster, head of forex at Citibank Australia, commented, "They (the Swiss) started talking down the currency 10 big figures ago so they must be pretty happy with the way it's going."
"In fact, I'm surprised the market took so long today to sell on the latest official encouragement."
"The fundamentals strongly favour a higher dollar and, although we'll probably get a correction in a figure or two, for the moment everyone wants to buy," he added.

He noted low Swiss interest rates and official sanction for a depreciating currency made it very attractive to borrow in Swiss francs and lend in higher yielding currencies, thus making the yield differential and a capital gain on the currency.
The Swiss franc was weaker on the crosses as well. At 0312 GMT, the mark was quoted at 0.8689/92 centimes compared with Monday's finish in Zurich of 86.37/39 centimes.
Against the yen, it was quoted at 83.42/47 at 0323 GMT.

A Swiss/yen dealer with a Japanese trust bank in Tokyo said the trend of the Swiss franc was likely to be a gentle weakening, due to fundamental economic conditions and the lingering possibility of another rate cut.

"At this point, it's not entirely out of the question that there may be another interest rate cut in Switzerland, with the narrowing interest rate differential likely to dampen Japanese investors' interest in holding Swiss-denominated assets," he said.
But he added such a downtrend could be reversed should concerns rise about the overall health of the Japanese banking system, which would be likely to lead the yen lower.

Rumours a Japanese bank had suffered losses in derivatives trading, later denied, along with a ratings downgrade of several Japanese banks by Moody's, buoyed most currencies slightly against the yen in Tokyo cross-trading on Monday.

The trust bank dealer said that he saw the Swiss franc trading from 82.00 yen to 82.50 yen in a month's time, and around 81.00 yen by the end of March. Japanese investors usually repatriate funds ahead of end-March book closings.
-- Singapore newsroom (65) 870-3080
